definition: Pythia is an ancient text restoration model that recovers missing characters from damaged text input using deep neural networks.
details: It was created by Yannis Assael, Thea Sommerschield, and Jonathan Prag, researchers from Google DeepMind and the University of Oxford. To study the society and the history of ancient civilisations, ancient history relies on disciplines such as epigraphy, the study of ancient inscribed texts. Hundreds of thousands of these texts, known as inscriptions, have survived to our day, but are often damaged over the centuries. Illegible parts of the text must then be restored by specialists, called epigraphists, in order to extract meaningful information from the text and use it to expand our knowledge of the context in which the text was written. Pythia takes as input the damaged text, and is trained to return hypothesised restorations of ancient Greek inscriptions, working as an assistive aid for ancient historians. Its neural network architecture works at both the character- and word-level, thereby effectively handling long-term context information, and dealing efficiently with incomplete word representations. Pythia is applicable to any discipline dealing with ancient texts (philology, papyrology, codicology) and can work in any language (ancient or modern).

explainer.lead: Pythia recovers missing characters in damaged ancient inscriptions, a task that otherwise depends on scarce specialist epigraphers. It matters because it makes large corpora of damaged texts usable for studying ancient societies.

tiers.eli5: Like a helper that guesses the faded letters in an old stone carving so historians can read the message again.
tiers.practitioner: The model takes the damaged text as input and predicts the illegible characters, plugging gaps that specialists would otherwise fill by hand; the pitfall is restoring text that fits the pattern but not the actual historical record.
tiers.paperLevel: A deep neural network maps a damaged character sequence to a restored one, filling in missing positions; accuracy is measured on how often the restored characters match the true text, and restoration remains probabilistic.

explainer.example: Given an inscription with several broken letters mid-line, Pythia proposes candidate characters for each gap, which epigraphers can then accept or reject.
